section.heading: Accessible Web applications and WAI-ARIAAccessible Web applications and WAI-ARIA

landmark.paragraph:
For a web page to be accessible all important semantics about the page's functionality must be available so that assistive technology can understand and process the content and adapt it for the user. However, as content becomes more and more complex, the standard HTML tags and attributes become inadequate in providing semantics reliably. Modern Web applications often apply scripts to elements to control their functionality and to enable them to act as a control or other dynamic component. These custom components or widgets do not provide a way to convey semantic information to the user agent. landmark.paragraph: Automated accessibility testing tools have become a widely used first step in identifying accessibility barriers on websites. Tools such as axe-core, WAVE, and Lighthouse evaluate a web page's Document Object Model (DOM) against rule sets derived from the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) and related standards, flagging violations such as missing alternative text, insufficient colour contrast, or absent form labels.Automated accessibility testing tools have become a widely used first step in identifying accessibility barriers on websites. Tools such as axe-core, WAVE, and Lighthouse evaluate a web page's Document Object Model (DOM) against rule sets derived from the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) and related standards, flagging violations such as missing alternative text, insufficient colour contrast, or absent form labels.

landmark.name: Limitations of static DOM analysis

section.heading: Limitations of static DOM analysisLimitations of static DOM analysis

landmark.paragraph: Most automated tools operate by inspecting the static structure of a web page — its HTML, ARIA attributes, and computed styles — without interacting with the page as a user would. This approach has inherent limitations in several areas.Most automated tools operate by inspecting the static structure of a web page — its HTML, ARIA attributes, and computed styles — without interacting with the page as a user would. This approach has inherent limitations in several areas.

A tool can confirm that a skip navigation link exists in the DOM, but cannot verify that activating it correctly moves keyboard focus to the main content area. Automated scans can reliably detect the presence of skip links or landmark regions, but verification that they function correctly requires behavioural testing.
Presence versus function.Presence versus function. A button labelled "click here" or an image with alt text reading "photo" satisfies the relevant automated rule while providing no useful information to a screen reader user. Distinguishing a name that exists from a name that communicates intent requires contextual judgement that deterministic rules cannot supply.
